people.short_bio: Girolamo Masci was the first Franciscan pope. Minister general of his order after St Bonaventure, he was elected in 1288 after a long vacancy and died in Rome in 1292.
people.long_bio: Born near Ascoli in the Marche, Girolamo Masci joined the Franciscans young and was sent on a mission to Constantinople in 1272. He succeeded St Bonaventure as minister general, became a cardinal in 1278 and bishop of Palestrina in 1281. As pope he crowned Charles II king of Sicily and Naples, granted the cardinals half of the revenues of the Apostolic See, and sent missionaries east, among them John of Montecorvino, who went on to China.

people.context: The late thirteenth century saw the papacy entangled in the struggle between the Angevins of Naples and the Aragonese over Sicily after the Sicilian Vespers of 1282. In 1291 Acre, the last crusader stronghold in the Holy Land, fell to the Mamluks. In Rome the Colonna and Orsini families competed for influence over the curia.

people.short_bio: A hermit of the Abruzzo mountains, Pietro del Morrone was elected pope in his eighties in 1294 to end a two-year deadlock. Overwhelmed by the office, he resigned after five months and died in custody in 1296.
people.long_bio: Of humble origins in Molise, Pietro became a Benedictine and then a hermit on Monte Morrone and the Maiella, gathering followers who became the Celestine congregation, approved by Urban IV in 1264. In July 1294 the cardinals, deadlocked at Perugia for over two years, unanimously chose him. He fell under the influence of Charles II of Naples and, after decreeing that a pope could resign, abdicated at Naples on 13 December 1294. His successor kept him confined at the castle of Fumone, where he died on 19 May 1296.

people.context: The papacy was caught between the Angevin kings of Naples and Roman baronial families. A deadlocked conclave left the see empty from 1292 to 1294. Spiritual movements stressing poverty and hoping for an 'angelic pope' greeted the hermit's election with enthusiasm.

people.short_bio: A canon lawyer from Anagni, Benedetto Caetani succeeded Celestine V in 1294. He proclaimed the first Jubilee in 1300 and clashed fiercely with Philip IV of France over papal authority.
people.long_bio: Benedetto Caetani studied canon and civil law and served as legate in France and Sicily before becoming a cardinal in 1281. Elected on 24 December 1294, he defended the rights of the Church against Philip IV of France in bulls such as Clericis laicos (1296) and Unam sanctam (1302), which asserted the supremacy of spiritual power. He proclaimed the Jubilee of 1300, which drew great crowds to Rome. In September 1303 agents of Philip, led by Guillaume de Nogaret with Sciarra Colonna, seized him at Anagni; freed by the townspeople, he returned to Rome and died there on 11 October 1303.

people.context: Strong national monarchies, above all Philip IV's France, now challenged papal claims to authority over kings, especially over taxing the clergy. In Rome the Caetani fought the Colonna family. The Anagni outrage of 1303 marked a turning point toward the papacy's later move to Avignon.

people.short_bio: A Dominican from Treviso and former master general of his order, Niccolò Boccasini was elected in 1303 after the death of Boniface VIII. He made peace with France but died suddenly at Perugia after eight months.
people.long_bio: Niccolò Boccasini joined the Dominicans at fourteen, became a lector in theology and was elected master general in 1296. Made a cardinal in 1298, he served as legate to Hungary and stood by Boniface VIII at Anagni. Elected unanimously on 22 October 1303, he worked for reconciliation with Philip IV of France, while excommunicating Nogaret and Sciarra Colonna for the attack on his predecessor. He died suddenly at Perugia on 7 July 1304; poisoning was suspected but never proved.

people.short_bio: A Gascon archbishop of Bordeaux, Bertrand de Got was elected in 1305 and never went to Rome. He settled the papal court at Avignon, beginning some seventy years of residence there.
people.long_bio: Bertrand de Got held church posts at Bordeaux, served as papal chaplain and was bishop of Comminges before becoming archbishop of Bordeaux. Elected in 1305 after a long conclave, he was crowned at Lyon and, after years moving around southern France, settled at Avignon in 1309. Under heavy pressure from Philip IV, he suppressed the Knights Templar at the Council of Vienne (1311-1312) without a formal condemnation of the order. He also promulgated the collection of decretals called the Clementines. He died at Roquemaure on 20 April 1314.

people.short_bio: A lawyer from Cahors, Jacques Duèse was elected at Lyon in 1316 aged about 67 and reigned for eighteen years from Avignon. He reorganised papal finances and fought long battles with Louis of Bavaria and the Spiritual Franciscans.
people.long_bio: Jacques Duèse taught canon and civil law, became bishop of Fréjus, chancellor to Charles II of Naples and cardinal-bishop of Porto. Elected at Lyon on 7 August 1316 after a two-year vacancy, he settled at Avignon and centralised church administration, expanding annates and other revenues. He excommunicated Louis of Bavaria, who had himself crowned in Rome and set up an antipope. He condemned the Spiritual Franciscans and in 1323 declared heretical the claim that Christ and the apostles owned nothing. His sermons suggesting that the saints see God only after the Last Judgment caused controversy; he withdrew the view before his death at Avignon on 4 December 1334.

people.long_bio: Jacques Fournier became a Cistercian, abbot of Fontfroide, then bishop of Pamiers (1317) and of Mirepoix, and a cardinal in 1327. As pope he issued the constitution Benedictus Deus (1336), defining that the souls of the just see God immediately after death, closing the controversy raised by his predecessor. He worked to reform religious orders and curb clerical abuses, and in 1339 began building the Palace of the Popes at Avignon. He died there on 25 April 1342.

people.short_bio: A Benedictine from the Limousin and a celebrated preacher, Pierre Roger was elected in 1342. He bought Avignon for the papacy, protected Jews during the Black Death and kept a splendid court.
people.long_bio: Pierre Roger entered the Benedictine abbey of La Chaise-Dieu, taught at Paris and rose to be abbot, archbishop and cardinal (1338). Elected at Avignon on 7 May 1342, he bought the city from Queen Joanna of Naples in 1348. When the Black Death struck in 1348-1349 he issued bulls protecting the Jews, who were being blamed for the plague, and offered them refuge. He granted a Jubilee for 1350, which brought huge numbers of pilgrims to Rome. His court was famous for its magnificence. He died at Avignon on 6 December 1352.

people.short_bio: A law professor from the Limousin, Étienne Aubert was elected at Avignon in 1352. He reformed the papal court and sent Cardinal Albornoz to win back the Papal States.
people.long_bio: Étienne Aubert taught civil law at Toulouse and became a senior judge there, then bishop of Noyon and of Clermont, cardinal and Grand Penitentiary. Elected on 18 December 1352, he sent clergy back to their posts, curbed abuses in benefices and reduced luxury at the papal court. Cardinal Gil de Albornoz, sent to Italy, restored papal authority in the Papal States, preparing the way for a return to Rome. He crowned Charles IV emperor in 1355 and helped bring about the Peace of Brétigny between France and England in 1360. He died at Avignon on 12 September 1362.

people.short_bio: A Benedictine abbot and canon lawyer, Guillaume de Grimoard was elected in 1362. He brought the papacy back to Rome in 1367, but returned to Avignon in 1370, where he died.
people.long_bio: Born into a knightly family at Grizac in the Languedoc, Guillaume de Grimoard became a Benedictine monk, a professor of canon law and a papal diplomat, and in 1352 an abbot. Elected in 1362 while not yet a cardinal, he kept a simple monastic life as pope. He worked for peace in Europe and for a crusade, excommunicated Bernabò Visconti of Milan and founded or supported universities, including Kraków and Vienna. In 1367 he moved the papacy back to Rome, staying about three years, but in September 1370 he returned to Avignon, where he died on 19 December 1370.

people.short_bio: Nephew of Clement VI, Pierre Roger de Beaufort was elected at Avignon in 1370. Urged on by St Catherine of Siena among others, he returned the papacy to Rome in 1377, and died there the following year.
people.long_bio: Pierre Roger de Beaufort received many benefices from his uncle Clement VI and was made a cardinal young. Elected at Avignon at the end of December 1370, he fought a costly war with Florence, placing the city under interdict. Encouraged by the prayers and letters of St Catherine of Siena, he moved the papal see back to Rome in January 1377. That year he condemned propositions of John Wyclif in five bulls. He died in Rome in March 1378. He was the last French pope, and the disputed election after his death began the Western Schism.

people.short_bio: Archbishop of Bari and head of the papal chancery, Bartolomeo Prignano was elected in Rome in 1378 amid popular pressure for an Italian pope. Within months most cardinals rejected him, beginning the Western Schism.
people.long_bio: Bartolomeo Prignano spent many years at Avignon, became archbishop of Acerenza in 1364 and of Bari in 1377, and ran the papal chancery. He was elected in April 1378, not being a cardinal, while Roman crowds demanded a Roman or at least Italian pope. His harsh attempts at reform alienated the cardinals, most of whom declared his election invalid and in September 1378 chose Robert of Geneva as Clement VII, who settled at Avignon. Urban had cardinals suspected of conspiracy imprisoned, and some were executed. He died in Rome on 15 October 1389.

people.context: After the disputed election of 1378 the Western Church split: one line of popes stayed in Rome, while a rival line backed by France resided at Avignon, and from 1409 a third line arose from the Council of Pisa. Kingdoms took sides by politics. The schism ended only at the Council of Constance (1414-1418).

people.short_bio: A Neapolitan of a noble but impoverished family, Pietro Tomacelli was elected by the Roman cardinals in 1389. He held Rome and the Papal States firmly, but the schism with Avignon continued throughout his reign.
people.long_bio: Elected in Rome on 2 November 1389 after the death of Urban VI, Pietro Tomacelli refused to abdicate in favour of the Avignon claimants Clement VII and Benedict XIII. He presided over Jubilee celebrations, including the Holy Year of 1400, won back many cities and strongholds of the Papal States, and secured Rome by fortifying Castel Sant'Angelo. To raise money he made annates a permanent tax, and he was accused of greed and nepotism. He died in Rome on 1 October 1404 after a failed meeting with envoys of Benedict XIII.

King Ladislaus of Naples helped him put down a Roman revolt, then extracted concessions and later supported rebels against him. He planned to restore the university of Rome shortly before his death on 6 November 1406.

people.short_bio: A Venetian noble, Angelo Correr was elected by the Roman cardinals in 1406, already about eighty, on condition that he abdicate if his rival did. In 1415 he resigned at the Council of Constance, opening the way to end the Western Schism.
people.long_bio: Angelo Correr was bishop of Castello, titular patriarch of Constantinople and a cardinal before his election on 30 November 1406. He pledged to resign if the Avignon claimant Benedict XIII did the same, but a planned meeting at Savona never took place. In 1409 the Council of Pisa declared both men deposed and elected a third claimant, which deepened the split. At the Council of Constance, his representative announced his resignation on 4 July 1415, and the council accepted it. He died at Recanati on 18 October 1417.

people.short_bio: A member of the Roman Colonna family, Oddone Colonna was elected at the Council of Constance in 1417, ending the Western Schism. He returned to a ruined Rome in 1420 and began rebuilding the city and the Papal States.
people.long_bio: Oddone Colonna was a cardinal when the Council of Constance, having set aside the three rival claimants, elected him unanimously on 11 November 1417. Reaching Rome in 1420, he found the city in ruins and set about restoring churches and order, laying foundations for the Roman Renaissance. He brought rebellious cities of the Papal States back under papal rule. As Constance had required, he summoned a council at Pavia in 1423, moved to Siena, and arranged the next at Basel. He also called for a crusade against the Hussites in Bohemia. He died in Rome on 20 February 1431.

people.context: The Council of Constance (1414-1418) ended the schism and condemned Jan Hus, who was burned in 1415. It also asserted that councils hold authority over popes, and required regular councils, setting up a long struggle between conciliarists and the papacy. In Bohemia the Hussite wars broke out after Hus's death.

people.short_bio: A Venetian and nephew of Gregory XII, Gabriele Condulmer was elected in 1431. He struggled with the Council of Basel, which deposed him, but achieved a short-lived union with the Greek Church at Florence in 1439.
people.long_bio: Gabriele Condulmer came from a wealthy Venetian family; his mother's brother was Gregory XII. Elected on 3 March 1431, he soon clashed with the Council of Basel, which defied his attempt to dissolve it and eventually declared him deposed in 1439. A revolt in Rome in 1434 forced him to flee down the Tiber, and he lived for years in Florence. He moved the council to Ferrara in 1437 and then to Florence, where union with the Greek Church was proclaimed on 5 July 1439. He returned to Rome in 1443 and died there on 23 February 1447.

people.short_bio: A humanist scholar from Sarzana, Tommaso Parentucelli was elected in 1447. He founded the Vatican Library, celebrated the Jubilee of 1450 and crowned Frederick III, the last emperor crowned in Rome.
people.long_bio: Tommaso Parentucelli worked as a tutor in Florentine families and for years served Cardinal Niccolò Albergati, collecting books and meeting humanist scholars. He became a cardinal in December 1446 and was elected pope on 6 March 1447. He gathered thousands of manuscripts, founding the Vatican Library, and planned the rebuilding of Rome. The Jubilee of 1450 celebrated the end of the schism with Basel. In 1452 he crowned Frederick III emperor in Rome. After Constantinople fell in 1453 he proclaimed a crusade. He died in Rome in March 1455.

people.short_bio: A Valencian lawyer, Alfonso de Borja was elected in 1455 aged 76. He poured his energy into a crusade against the Turks and ordered the retrial that cleared Joan of Arc.
people.long_bio: Alfonso de Borja once supported the Avignon claimant Benedict XIII but later helped bring about the submission of Clement VIII to Martin V. He became bishop of Valencia in 1429 and cardinal in 1444, and was elected pope on 8 April 1455. Determined to answer the fall of Constantinople, he sent preachers and envoys and ordered the noon bell for prayer; in 1456 crusaders defeated the Turks at Belgrade, though Europe's rulers gave little help. He ordered the retrial that declared Joan of Arc innocent. He raised his nephews, including Rodrigo, later Alexander VI, to high office. He died in Rome on 6 August 1458.

people.long_bio: Enea Silvio Piccolomini was a secretary at the Council of Basel and then poet and secretary to Emperor Frederick III, writing widely read works. Later ordained, he became bishop of Trieste and of Siena, and a cardinal in 1456. As pope he summoned the Congress of Mantua (1459) to organise a crusade, and in the bull Execrabilis (1460) condemned appeals from the pope to a future council. He canonized St Catherine of Siena and rebuilt his birthplace as the town of Pienza. He died at Ancona on 14 August 1464 while preparing to lead the crusade himself.

people.short_bio: A Venetian nobleman and nephew of Eugene IV, Pietro Barbo was elected in 1464. He built the Palazzo Venezia in Rome, clashed with humanists of the Roman Academy, and fixed the Jubilee at every 25 years.
people.long_bio: Pietro Barbo, son of Niccolò Barbo and Polissena Condulmer, was the nephew of Eugene IV, who advanced his career in the Church. Elected on 30 August 1464, he suppressed the college of abbreviators in 1466 and the Roman Academy, whose members he accused of pagan ways. He built the Palace of San Marco, today's Palazzo Venezia, sponsored lavish carnival festivities and revised Rome's statutes. In 1470 he decreed that a Jubilee be held every twenty-five years. He also protected universities and favoured the new art of printing. He died in Rome on 26 July 1471.

people.short_bio: A Genoese, Giovanni Battista Cibo was elected in 1484. His reign saw a long conflict with Naples, the custody of the Ottoman prince Djem in Rome, and the fall of Granada in 1492.
people.long_bio: Son of Aran Cibo, a Roman senator, Giovanni Battista had two illegitimate children before taking orders. He became bishop of Savona and then Molfetta, and a cardinal in 1473. Elected on 29 August 1484, he issued a bull on witchcraft in December of that year. A long quarrel with King Ferrante of Naples frustrated his plans for a crusade, though the Ottoman prince Djem, held in Rome, gave some leverage over the sultan. The fall of Granada in 1491-1492 completed the Spanish reconquest. He died in Rome on 25 July 1492.

people.short_bio: Nephew of Callixtus III, Rodrigo Borgia served for decades as vice-chancellor before his election in 1492. His reign is remembered for nepotism and for the ambitions of his children, above all Cesare Borgia.
people.long_bio: Born at Xàtiva near Valencia, Rodrigo was made a cardinal by his uncle Callixtus III in 1456 and vice-chancellor of the Roman Church, an office he held for decades. Elected on 11 August 1492, amid widespread rumours of simony, he openly advanced his children by Vannozza Cattanei: Juan, Cesare, Lucrezia and Jofre. In 1493 he drew a line of demarcation between Spanish and Portuguese claims in the newly discovered lands. He faced the French invasion of Italy by Charles VIII in 1494, celebrated the Jubilee of 1500, and backed Cesare's conquest of the Romagna. He died in Rome on 18 August 1503, probably of fever.

people.short_bio: Son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, Giovanni de' Medici was made a cardinal at 13 and elected pope in 1513. A great patron of the arts, he reigned as Martin Luther's protest began.
people.long_bio: The second son of Lorenzo de' Medici and Clarice Orsini, Giovanni was created a cardinal in 1489 aged thirteen. Elected in March 1513, he continued the Fifth Lateran Council, whose reform decrees were little enforced, and in 1516 agreed the Concordat of Bologna with Francis I of France. His court was famous for its patronage of artists and scholars, including Raphael. The preaching of indulgences to fund the new St Peter's provoked criticism, and in 1517 Martin Luther's protest launched the Reformation. Leo condemned Luther's teachings in 1520 and excommunicated him in 1521. He died in Rome on 1 December 1521.

people.short_bio: A Dutch theologian and former tutor of Charles V, Adriaan Florensz was elected in 1522 while regent of Spain. He tried to reform the curia and openly admitted its faults, but died after twenty months.
people.long_bio: Born in Utrecht, the son of Florens, Adriaan studied at Louvain, became a doctor of theology in 1491 and taught there. From 1506 he tutored the young Charles, later Emperor Charles V, and in Spain he became grand inquisitor, cardinal and regent. Elected in his absence on 9 January 1522, he worked to cut papal spending and reform the curia, publicly acknowledging that corruption had spread from the Roman court. He appealed in vain for help for Rhodes, which fell to the Turks in 1522. He died in Rome on 14 September 1523. He was the last non-Italian pope until John Paul II.

people.short_bio: Cousin of Leo X, Giulio de' Medici was elected in 1523. His shifting alliances led to the Sack of Rome in 1527, and he refused Henry VIII's request to annul his marriage.
people.long_bio: Giulio was the son of Giuliano de' Medici, killed in Florence in 1478, and was raised by his uncle Lorenzo the Magnificent. Elected on 19 November 1523, he joined France, Venice and Florence in the League of Cognac (1526) against Charles V. In May 1527 imperial troops sacked Rome, and the pope was besieged in Castel Sant'Angelo. He later made peace with Charles and crowned him emperor at Bologna in 1530. His refusal to annul Henry VIII's marriage to Catherine of Aragon led to England's break with Rome. He commissioned Michelangelo's Last Judgment. He died on 25 September 1534.

people.short_bio: A Roman noble of the Farnese family, cardinal for over forty years, Alessandro Farnese was elected in 1534. He opened the Council of Trent in 1545 and launched the Catholic reform, while also advancing his own family.
people.long_bio: Alessandro Farnese was made a cardinal-deacon in 1493 and was elected pope on 13 October 1534. He named reforming cardinals, approved the Society of Jesus in 1540 and set up the Roman Inquisition in 1542. After long efforts he opened the Council of Trent, which held its first session on 13 December 1545. A generous patron, he commissioned Michelangelo's work in the Sistine Chapel and on St Peter's. He also practised open nepotism, making two teenage grandsons cardinals and creating the duchy of Parma and Piacenza for his son Pier Luigi. He died at the Quirinal on 10 November 1549.

people.short_bio: A Roman lawyer who had presided over the opening of the Council of Trent, Giovanni Maria del Monte was elected in 1550. He reopened the council in 1551, but is also remembered for his villa and his nepotism.

Elected in February 1550, he ordered the council to resume at Trent in 1551 after its move to Bologna, before war forced its suspension again. In 1552 he issued the founding bull of the Collegium Germanicum for training German priests. He sent Cardinal Reginald Pole to support the Catholic restoration in England under Mary I. He built the Villa Giulia outside the Porta del Popolo, and his promotion of the young Innocenzo del Monte to cardinal caused scandal. He died in Rome on 23 March 1555.

people.long_bio: Antonio Ghislieri took the name Michele as a Dominican, was ordained in 1528 and taught theology for many years. He served as inquisitor in Lombardy and became inquisitor general and cardinal in 1557. Elected on 7 January 1566, he lived austerely and enforced the discipline of Trent, publishing the Roman Catechism, the reformed Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (1570). He excommunicated Elizabeth I of England. He formed the Holy League whose fleet defeated the Ottomans at Lepanto on 7 October 1571, and instituted a feast of Our Lady of Victory, later the Rosary. He died in Rome on 1 May 1572.

people.long_bio: Ugo Boncompagni taught law at Bologna and took part in the Council of Trent as a papal jurist. Elected on 13 May 1572, he founded and endowed many colleges and seminaries, many entrusted to the Jesuits, and in 1582 built the great building of the Roman College, today's Gregorian University. He issued an official edition of canon law and a revised Roman Martyrology. His reform of the Julian calendar took effect in October 1582. He ordered celebrations in Rome after the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572, though he had no part in it. In 1585 he received an embassy of four young Japanese Christians. He died in Rome on 10 April 1585.

people.short_bio: A Franciscan of humble origins from the Marche, Felice Peretti was elected in 1585. In five years he crushed banditry, restored papal finances, reorganised the Curia into fifteen congregations and transformed the city of Rome.
people.long_bio: Felice Peretti entered the Franciscan friary at Montalto at twelve, was ordained in 1547 and became procurator general of his order. Elected on 24 April 1585, he suppressed the brigands of the Papal States and filled the empty treasury. In 1586 he fixed the College of Cardinals at seventy, and in 1588 created fifteen permanent congregations of cardinals to run the Church and the Papal States. He completed the dome of St Peter's, built the Vatican Library building, raised obelisks in key squares and brought water to Rome by the Acqua Felice. He died at the Quirinal on 27 August 1590.
actions: Reorganised the Curia into 15 congregations (1588)

people.context: The Council of Trent (1545-1563) answered the Protestant Reformation by defining Catholic doctrine and ordering reforms of bishops, clergy and seminaries. Popes of the following decades enforced its decrees, reorganised the Roman Curia and supported new orders such as the Jesuits. Europe was divided by wars of religion, especially in France and the Low Countries, while Spain under Philip II was the leading Catholic power and the Ottoman threat continued in the Mediterranean.

people.short_bio: A Roman canonist and experienced diplomat, Giambattista Castagna was elected on 15 September 1590 and died twelve days later, before his coronation. His is the shortest papal reign on record.
people.long_bio: Giambattista Castagna became archbishop of Rossano in 1553 and served about seven years as nuncio at the court of Philip II of Spain, later as nuncio in Venice, and as inquisitor general from 1586. Elected on 15 September 1590, he showed concern for Rome's poor, ordering a list of those in need and paying the debts of the papal pawn banks. He fell ill a few days after his election and died on 27 September 1590, before being crowned.

people.short_bio: Bishop of Cremona and friend of St Charles Borromeo and St Philip Neri, Niccolò Sfondrati was elected in December 1590. In a reign of ten months he backed the Catholic League in France against Henry of Navarre.
people.long_bio: Niccolò Sfondrati was the son of a Milanese senator who later became a cardinal. Made bishop of Cremona in 1560, he was close to Charles Borromeo and Philip Neri. Elected on 5 December 1590, he supported the Catholic League in France, renewing the excommunication of Henry of Navarre in March 1591 and sending money and papal troops under his nephew Ercole. He raised the congregation of St Camillus de Lellis to a religious order, banned betting on papal elections, and ordered reparations to the peoples of the Philippines. He died in Rome on 16 October 1591.

people.context: France was torn by the Wars of Religion: the Protestant Henry of Navarre claimed the throne after 1589, opposed by the Catholic League with Spanish support. Rome had just seen a rapid succession of popes in 1590, and famine and disease afflicted central Italy.
